title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
authors: Nonchev, K.; Jang, Y.; Nlandu Khodo, S.; Koelzer, V. H.; Raetsch, G.; Moor, M. B.
abstract: IntroductionSpatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. MethodsWe adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1 534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. ResultsKidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each models 1 000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman{rho} , 0.64). ConclusionsKidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives. Translational StatementSpatial molecular profiling of kidney biopsies is informative but too costly for routine use, whereas hematoxylin and eosin sections exist for nearly every biopsy. We show that a model adapted to paired kidney histology and spatial transcriptomics infers programs of tubular injury, metabolic differentiation, and fibrosis from routine histology, and that these programs track kidney function and pathology across 476 participants. Applied to existing archives, virtual spatial transcriptomics could stratify heterogeneous patients by tissue molecular state, prioritize biopsies for targeted assays, and support biomarker discovery and trial enrichment once validated prospectively.

infographic.key_insight: Kidney-adapted AI predicted spatial gene expression from routine histology, linking tissue features to injury, repair, and fibrosis-associated molecular programs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This kidney disease study—not cancer drug discovery—could extend molecular characterization to archived biopsies, but does not establish clinical diagnostic utility.
method: Adapted DeepSpot-M using paired histology and spatial transcriptomics from 209 KPMP participants.
Evaluated predictions in held-out human biopsies and 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures.
Generated 5.46 million virtual spots from 1,534 slides covering 476 additional KPMP participants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Mean gene-expression prediction correlation improved from 0.22 to 0.43 for each model’s 1,000 best-predicted genes; predictions preserved all 13 disease-marker differences and all 11 measured associations with eGFR.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted expression is not a direct molecular measurement; broader validation is needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs

title: An LLM-assisted Pipeline for Identifying ClinicalTrials.gov Registry Changes and Their Association with Primary Endpoint Positivity
authors: Purevdorj, A.; Dennstaedt, F.; Zwahlen, D. R.; Windisch, P.
abstract: Registration of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) in a public registry such as ClinicalTrials.gov should minimize the risk of reporting bias. However, records may be modified during a trial and the resulting discrepancies are not always apparent without a detailed examination of all version histories, a process that is cumbersome when performed manually. We developed an automated workflow to investigate whether specific changes to RCT registry entries are associated with primary endpoint positivity. Our pipeline extracts RCT records from ClinicalTrials.gov and systematically detects changes between successive versions using a combination of deterministic textual analysis and large language model (LLM)-assisted classification. We could show a positive association between trial positivity and changes to primary outcomes (OR 1.91; 95% CI 1.48-2.47) as well as to arms and interventions (OR 2.10; 95% CI 1.62-2.73). Associations were weaker when changes occurred exclusively before the primary completion date, pointing to the importance of timing in evaluating potentially consequential modifications to RCT design. Our automated pipeline can enable analysis of trial registration records at scale, facilitating the work of reviewers and meta-scientists to promote research integrity.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM-assisted analysis linked changes in trial registry entries to higher odds of primary endpoint positivity, without establishing causation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This trial-transparency research, rather than cancer drug discovery, could help reviewers identify registry changes warranting closer scrutiny.
method: Extract randomized clinical trial records from ClinicalTrials.gov.
Detect changes across successive versions using deterministic text analysis and LLM-assisted classification.
Assess associations with primary endpoint positivity and the timing of changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Primary outcome changes were associated with endpoint positivity (OR 1.91; 95% CI 1.48–2.47), as were arm/intervention changes (OR 2.10; 95% CI 1.62–2.73); associations were weaker for changes occurring exclusively before primary completion.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report sample size or LLM classification accuracy, limiting assessment of robustness.
infographic.paper_title: An LLM-assisted Pipeline for Identifying ClinicalTrials.gov Registry Changes and Their Association with Primary Endpoint Positivity

title: Prospective prediction of clinical trial outcomes from public evidence
authors: Xu, J.; Zhang, W.; Yuan, Y.; Wu, C.
abstract: Predicting clinical trial outcomes requires interpreting biological and clinical evidence in the context of a specific intervention, population and study design. Here we test whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can predict trial outcomes from publicly available evidence. We introduce TrialDossier, which assembles standardized evidence dossiers, and TrialOutlook, which uses these dossiers with GPT-5 to estimate the probability that a trial meets its prespecified primary endpoint. Among 694 ongoing trials with results expected within six months of cohort assembly, 69 outcomes first disclosed after forecast recording had been adjudicated by 20 October 2026. TrialOutlook achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.819 (95% confidence interval, 0.708-0.914) and an average precision of 0.860. TrialOutlook correctly identified 27 of 29 failures (93.1%) and incorrectly classified 17 of 40 successes as failures. We further recorded forecasts for 5,809 ongoing trials associated with US-listed companies and established a public benchmark linking archived evidence and fixed forecasts to adjudicated outcomes as they become available.

infographic.key_insight: An evidence-based GPT-5 workflow showed promising prospective prediction of clinical trial outcomes, rather than cancer drug discovery specifically.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support trial research prioritization, but does not establish treatment efficacy or guide individual patient care.
method: TrialDossier assembles standardized dossiers from public evidence.
TrialOutlook uses GPT-5 to estimate whether trials will meet prespecified primary endpoints.
Fixed forecasts are linked to subsequently disclosed, adjudicated outcomes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 69 adjudicated outcomes from 694 ongoing trials, AUROC was 0.819 (95% CI, 0.708–0.914) and average precision was 0.860; 27 of 29 failures were identified, but 17 of 40 successes were classified as failures.
infographic.watch_item: Only 69 outcomes were adjudicated, and the substantial misclassification of successful trials warrants caution before operational use.
infographic.paper_title: Prospective prediction of clinical trial outcomes from public evidence

title: Early-life hallmarks of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity
authors: Tsang, R. S. M.; Stow, D.; Katzourou, I. K.; LINC Consortium, ; van den Bree, M. B. M.; Khandaker, G. M.; Timpson, N. J.
abstract: BackgroundInternalizing disorders and cardiometabolic disease are common conditions that frequently co-occur in later life and may be attributed to shared genetic influences. While phenotypic effects of polygenic liability of adult disorders may emerge early in life, studies have not investigated this in the context of multimorbidity. This study set out to investigate early manifestations of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity (ICM-MM) in a UK population birth cohort. MethodsWe used data from 5,934 individuals in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC). We modelled trajectories of 12 mental and cardiometabolic health outcomes using mixed effects models, and investigated effects of adult ICM-MM polygenic liability on these trajectories. We also investigated associations of adult ICM-MM polygenic liability with circulating inflammatory proteins (Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel) at ages 9 and 24. ResultsAdult ICM-MM polygenic liability is associated with cardiometabolic traits and inflammation, and with changes in depressive symptoms and cardiometabolic traits over time in childhood through to early adulthood. A notable early life biological footprint is inflammation. We found that higher ICM-MM polygenic liability is consistently associated with higher interleukin-6 (IL6), tumor necrosis family superfamily member 14 (TNFSF14) and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) levels in both childhood and early adulthood. ConclusionsAdult ICM-MM polygenic liability manifests early in life through changes in mental and cardiometabolic health and blood biomarkers, especially in increases of circulating inflammatory proteins related to obesity, immune cell chemotaxis and migration that may contribute to disease pathogenesis by seeding inflammation in relevant tissues.

infographic.key_insight: Genetic liability to adult internalizing–cardiometabolic multimorbidity is associated with early-life health changes and higher circulating inflammatory proteins.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings highlight potential early biological markers of shared mental and cardiometabolic disease liability, but do not establish clinical screening or treatment utility.
method: Analyzed 5,934 participants in the UK ALSPAC birth cohort.
Used mixed-effects models to assess associations between polygenic liability and trajectories of 12 mental and cardiometabolic outcomes.
Tested associations with circulating inflammatory proteins at ages 9 and 24 using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel.
infographic.evidence_signal: Higher polygenic liability was consistently associated with higher IL6, TNFSF14 and HGF levels at both ages 9 and 24.
infographic.watch_item: This observational cohort study does not establish causality or evaluate AI, cancer drug discovery, or clinical interventions.
infographic.paper_title: Early-life hallmarks of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity

title: ADSMoE: A mixture-of-experts-based transformer autoencoder for discovering multimodal Alzheimer's disease subtypes
authors: Meng, W.; Pan, J.; Yin, M.; Zhuang, P.; Gong, K.; Lin, M.; Xu, J.; Burns, M.; Wu, Y.; Yin, R.
abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD) exhibits substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity, posing critical challenges for advancing precision medicine. Existing data-driven approaches often rely on modality-specific clustering or predefined biomarker trajectories, limiting their ability to discover disease subtypes from incomplete, heterogeneous real-world data. In this study, we introduce ADSMoE, a mixture-of-experts (MoE)-based multimodal representation learning framework that jointly identifies AD subtypes as latent disease signatures while accommodating incomplete modality combinations. ADSMoE integrates a Fleximodal MoE encoder that accommodates arbitrary combinations of available modalities with a novel subtype-specific MoE decoder to capture complementary disease characteristics through expert specialization. Using data from 5,422 participants across three independent cohorts, we trained ADSMoE on the ADNI cohort and externally validated the identified subtypes in NACC and UKB without model retraining. The proposed ADSMoE identified four AD subtypes with distinct neuroimaging patterns, genetic and proteomic associations, and clinical characteristics. Benchmarking analyses demonstrated robust subtype discovery and strong biological and clinical relevance, while external validation revealed consistent subtype-associated characteristics across independent cohorts. ADSMoE advances AD subtyping by uncovering biologically and clinically meaningful AD heterogeneity from incomplete multimodal data, providing a scalable framework for disease stratification, biomarker discovery, and future precision medicine applications in AD.

infographic.key_insight: ADSMoE identified four biologically and clinically distinct Alzheimer’s disease subtypes from incomplete multimodal data.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The subtypes could support future Alzheimer’s disease stratification and biomarker research, but clinical utility is not established.
method: Uses a mixture-of-experts transformer autoencoder to learn multimodal disease signatures.
Handles varying combinations of available modalities with a Fleximodal MoE encoder.
Captures complementary subtype characteristics with a subtype-specific MoE decoder.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 5,422 participants in three cohorts, ADSMoE was trained on ADNI and externally validated in NACC and UKB without retraining, showing consistent subtype-associated characteristics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether subtype assignments improve prospective clinical decisions or treatment outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: ADSMoE: A mixture-of-experts-based transformer autoencoder for discovering multimodal Alzheimer's disease subtypes

title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
authors: Fathi Kazerooni, A.; Batal, F.; Vunnava, B.; Damaraju, E.; Tavallaii, A.; Gandhi, D.; Gottipati, A.; Zhu, P.; Chrysochoou, D.; Varshochi, S.; Adib Moradi, S.; Familiar, A. M.; Chiang, A.; Vaghani, Y.; Azemi, G.; Doig, M.; To, M.-S.; Luck, A.; Kim, M. C.; Khalili, N.; Khalili, N.; Jain, P.; Lee, C.; Hansford, J. R.; Di Ieva, A.; Storm, P. B.; Resnick, A. C.; Reddy, K.; Vossough, A.; Nabavizadeh, A.
abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

infographic.key_insight: PedDx classifies pediatric posterior fossa tumors from MRI, with higher accuracy among cases retained after confidence-based abstention.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This diagnostic AI research—not drug discovery—could inform future pediatric tumor assessment, but does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Uses T2-weighted MRI and pretrained 3DINO representations without tumor segmentation.
Combines calibrated predictions with confidence-based abstention.
Tests external reproducibility through an independently executed agentic workflow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases; accuracy rose from 79.8%, 81.4%, and 92.5% to 90.5%, 88.7%, and 97.3%, respectively, among non-abstained cases.
infographic.watch_item: Out-of-distribution inputs produced confidently incorrect predictions, and imaging perturbations exposed acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities.
infographic.paper_title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
